rows.description: It is not my problem, I tell myself, and turn away. Not caring is comfortable but leaves someone alone. Indifference grows when everyone thinks someone else will help, so I can be the one who helps.
My friend nudges me to join in mocking a classmate. I feel torn between fitting in and doing right. Wise: say I do not want to and walk off; real friends respect that, and it may make him think.
I am scared that if I speak up, I will be next. That fear is real and valid. Safe choices exist: report anonymously, tell a teacher later, be kind to the target afterward. Silence forever is heavier.
Someone sat next to me after I was teased and asked if I was okay. That tiny kindness meant more than words. I am not alone, and I can pass that kindness on later.
The leader grants and withdraws warmth to keep me anxious and obedient. Wise: notice the pattern, refuse tests of loyalty, and build friendships that are steady and kind.
They go silent when I approach and laugh over inside jokes. It hurts and is more about their insecurity than my worth. Wise: leave with dignity, find other groups, and tell someone I trust.
I watch the group freeze someone out and stay silent, feeling ashamed. Wise: quietly befriend the excluded person or speak up in a small way. Harmful: joining in to stay safe.
After weeks of feeling on the edge, I am invited in and feel relief mixed with wariness. Wise: enjoy it without dropping older friends or my values.
I want arts or design but my family expects science and engineering. Wise: research real paths, show numbers, ask for a trial period. Harmful: sulking or secret rebellion.
At family gatherings I am compared with a cousin who got into a top college. I feel small and angry. Wise: smile, answer briefly, and avoid making my path a contest.
I know my parents sacrifice for my future and feel both indebted and trapped. Wise: honour their effort while telling them my honest interests. Gratitude does not need to erase my choices.
I do not know what I want and the deadline makes me panic. Wise: try small experiments, talk to people in real jobs, and accept that the first choice can be revised.
People mock a photo of me and make it a meme. Shame flares. Wise: it is their cruelty, not my failing; report, block, lean on friends, and remember the internet forgets faster than it seems.

My old post went viral for the wrong reasons and strangers are abusing me. I feel sick and exposed. Wise: do not reply in heat, mute, save evidence, tell someone close, report threats. Harmful: staying up all night refreshing.
I follow a loud creator who says what I feel, and his attacks on others feel thrilling. Wise: enjoy his ideas, notice when he feeds on anger, and question anyone who profits from my outrage.

I stay up arguing with a stranger who will never change his mind. Wise: ask whether this exchange serves anyone; disengage, spend energy on offline action. Harmful: doomscrolling and hostile posts that hurt me too.
I see a child begging at a signal and feel a tug in my heart. Wanting to help is good. I can ask my parents about safe ways, like giving food or supporting an organisation.
I cannot afford the class trip and feel embarrassed. It is not my shame to carry. I can talk privately to a teacher, who may find quiet help, and my worth does not depend on money.
A classmate has a big house and gadgets, and I feel small. Envy is normal; I try to see my own gifts, and remember that wealth does not make anyone better or happier.
A richer friend shares his tiffin and does not make a show of it. I feel grateful and a bit awkward. I can accept warmly and share something of my own in return.
I moved to a new city and am teased for my language and food. Wise: keep my roots, learn the local ways gradually, and find one or two allies.
A classmate makes remarks about my caste, religion, region or family income. I feel small and angry. Wise: it is their bias, not my truth; tell a teacher and stay with friends who respect me.
A friend faces a bigoted remark and I hesitate to speak. Wise: a small stand like saying that isn't okay, or checking on them later, can matter greatly.
I look down on classmates who are poorer or on scholarships. Wise: notice how privilege shapes me and treat people by who they are.
